title: From Translation to Transformation: Paula Reichenberg on AI, Legal Quality, and the Future of Good Enough
author: Paula Reichenberg

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The excerpt promotes curated, compact legal-tech demonstrations and says they aid rapid product evaluation, but it provides no substantive position on workflow fit, organisational readiness, renewal economics, consumption costs, governance, or realized value. It therefore neither supports nor challenges the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: At these new LTH events, which are free to attend, by the way, you can log in virtually to see 12 curated providers offer demos of their products.
Greg Lambert (01:30)  And having these very compacted ⁓ demonstrations really helps people like me to evaluate things very quickly.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Reichenberg’s luxury-market analogy does not address whether legal AI benefits depend on organisational adaptation or human control. It suggests a possible premium positioning for law firms and legal-tech businesses, but offers no developed argument about implementation, workforce, judgment, pricing, or measured effects.
qs: So yes, I am looking forward to discovering the Loro Piana of both the law firms and the legal tech world.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Reichenberg accepts the value of legal-specific systems and materially extends the cluster with an operational case: a translation provider defended its specialist position by developing proprietary Swiss legal models, internalising multilingual legal-data processes and building in-house technical capability. The source does not, however, establish the cluster’s copilot and human-verification proposition.
qs: So we started developing our own Swiss legal translation models with external partners.
If you don’t have good data, you cannot build good models.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Reichenberg accepts the cluster’s core account of imperfect, selectively useful AI requiring professional verification and operating-model redesign. She materially extends it with a concrete “last mile” model centred on specialised data, correction workflows, simple interfaces and multidisciplinary legal-linguistic-engineering teams, while adding jurisdictional fragmentation and user over-trust as deployment constraints.
qs: Work with large language models, fine, but work with them through processes and data.
But our system tells you where they are and helps you to correct them, helps you to spot them.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Reichenberg supports the cluster’s emphasis on filtering rather than continuously chasing developments: she describes the technology news cycle as potentially consuming the whole night and recommends deliberately switching to non-technology content. Her reported agent-replacement claim also remains explicitly untested, consistent with the cluster’s caution toward anecdotal market claims.
qs: I’m not sure it’s a magic tool, but I think if you want to keep up with everything that’s happening, and everything is just so interesting, you can stay up all night reading through so many interesting news items everywhere.
So sometimes switching to some sort of meditation or relaxation podcast is my boring tip.

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that an evolving legal-tech market creates demand for structured market awareness. Its curated product demonstrations offer buyers a practical way to track new products and features, but the promotional announcement does not assess adoption, value, implementation quality or comparative performance, so it does not materially extend the cluster’s proposition.
qs: At these new LTH events, which are free to attend, by the way, you can log in virtually to see 12 curated providers offer demos of their products.
It’s an easy way to get up to date on what’s new in the market, whether that is brand new products or existing ones with new features.

kp.k: Machine translation shifted services toward premium specialist work
kp.d: Reichenberg reports that machine translation eliminated easy assignments and associated urgency fees at Hieronymus as clients handled average work themselves. The remaining business became highly specialized and could charge a premium; she sold it to a larger group pursuing industry-specific, high-quality services. She presents this experience as an analogy for potential legal-market restructuring, rather than evidence that the same transformation has already occurred across law firms.
qs: A lot of easy assignments, where we could at the time also bill huge urgency fees, those were the times, all disappeared.
Everything that could be average got totally taken over by the clients themselves.
It became a little jewel of highly specialized people who could then charge a premium, while average work was replaced, unfortunately, by this do-it-yourself behavior of the end clients.

kp.k: Clients accept imperfect AI contracts instead of hiring lawyers
kp.d: Reichenberg describes receiving AI-generated contracts directly from lay counterparties in recent negotiations, where lawyers previously would have been involved. She says she corrects provisions disadvantageous to her while leaving advantageous ones intact. Her account suggests client substitution and tolerance of mediocre output, but is anecdotal rather than a measured estimate of displacement or contractual consequences.
qs: This do-it-yourself attitude, before, we would have involved a lawyer to do that.
I change what is to my disadvantage, I leave what is to my advantage, and we sign it.
The problem is that it is creating a lot of mediocre outputs, but no one really cares about mediocrity in most cases.

kp.k: Professional quality requires processes and data beyond model improvements
kp.d: Reichenberg contrasts lay expectations that successive models will become perfect and replace lawyers with professionals' ability to detect persistent mistakes. Drawing on developing Swiss legal translation models, she argues that high-quality data and structured processes address the difficult last mile. She describes internalizing multilingual legal-data management and creating Neur.on to pursue this approach.
qs: If you don’t have good data, you cannot build good models.
So they think the next version is just going to be better and the next one is going to be perfect.
How do you solve this last mile that lay people don’t see, but as a professional you enjoy the tool, you see the mistakes, and you think, how can we become more efficient than this?
Work with large language models, fine, but work with them through processes and data.

kp.k: Verification support, not error elimination, defines product value
kp.d: Reichenberg explicitly rejects customers' expectation of perfect translations from her product. She positions its value as helping lawyers identify and correct errors, including propagating corrections, when outputs must be accurate enough for court submission. Her example contrasts a customer's reported 16 hours of correction with a claimed four hours using her system; this is a vendor's illustrative counterfactual, not a reported controlled evaluation.
qs: Our models, the only thing we guarantee is that they make mistakes. Guaranteed mistakes.
But our system tells you where they are and helps you to correct them, helps you to spot them. Instead of 16 hours, you would have spent four hours.
So you get the impression that you’re doing an intern’s work, but you know it’s super important because you cannot submit something wrong to the court.

kp.k: Basic chat dominates usage despite specialized productivity features
kp.d: Reichenberg says users frequently overlook features that could save time: she describes 80 percent of people using the chat window and separately says eighty percent of usage remains on the simplest functionality. No sample, measurement period or methodology is supplied. This behavior forced greater investment in basic functionality; she says experienced users and customers who have suffered lengthy correction work more readily recognize the product's value.
qs: most people, 80 percent of the people, just use the chat window and do everything there.
Eighty percent of usage is still on the absolutely simplest thing. So we had to put a lot more effort than we would have imagined into improving the basics.
But not everyone, if you have not gone through the pain, you will not get it.

kp.k: Balanced multidisciplinary teams support legal AI development
kp.d: Reichenberg attributes her team's effectiveness to combining legal, linguistic and engineering expertise from the founding stage, with trust and communication sustained as the team grows. She considers this balance uncommon among legal-tech founders she encounters. This is an organizational lesson from her experience, not comparative evidence of team performance.
qs: We started fresh with exactly one engineer, one linguist, and one lawyer.
When you build from that and you manage to have trust among the three founders who really represent those domains, then you grow the team with the same communication and the same bridges.
I hear from a lot of legal tech founders, and it is rare to have this triangle balanced.

kp.k: European legal AI must accommodate jurisdictional and linguistic fragmentation
kp.d: Reichenberg reports spinning Neur.on's multilingual legal natural-language-processing team into Noxtua, which she describes as a European sovereign alternative specializing in publishers' data across European countries. She emphasizes differences in legal traditions, languages and legal-system structures as development conditions. These are her descriptions of the companies and market, rather than independently demonstrated product capabilities.
qs: Now this team has been spun out into a European scale-up called Noxtua, which is offering a European sovereign alternative to non-European players, let’s put it like that, specialized as well in handling publishers’ data from every single European country.
Each jurisdiction really has a different legal tradition, different language, different structure of its legal system.

kp.k: Polished AI answers can command disproportionate client trust
kp.d: Reichenberg recounts a Swiss tax negotiation in which a foreign counterparty resisted a tax lawyer's explanation but accepted a ChatGPT answer after she corrected it. She links such reactions to polished presentation and perceived officialness. The episode illustrates her concern about clients' ability to appreciate professional expertise; it does not establish a population-wide trust pattern.
qs: We had a tax lawyer jump into the conversation and give us one hour of explanations and everything. They were still extremely reluctant to believe him.
ChatGPT came out with an answer, and I said, “Here it’s wrong, let’s correct it.” So that took five minutes, and they believed it.
They believed ChatGPT more than a professional.
There is no spelling mistake. It is just so polished.

kp.k: Quality could become a premium legal-market differentiator
kp.d: Reichenberg argues that tolerance for translation quality differs between luxury and mass-market businesses and predicts a comparable division in justice delivery: automated routine matters and premium human judging. Gebauer raises the access-to-justice implications of different levels of judicial commitment. These are analogies and speculative scenarios, not findings about an established two-tier court system.
qs: So language quality becomes a sign of luxury.

You can have the retail part for all your parking tickets, et cetera, and then you have the luxury part, where suddenly you have a human judge, who then maybe is a better judge than the average of today’s judges, who knows.
How much justice are you getting if you have one level and another level of commitment from the judicial system?

kp.k: AI interpretation may improve severely under-resourced access to justice
kp.d: Reichenberg offers a counterpoint to concerns about lower-quality automated justice: she describes refugees arriving in Italy served by interpreters paid $14 per hour and working too quickly to provide adequate care. She asserts that machine translation and language models now serve these people better than understaffed, underpaid human teams, while acknowledging imperfection. No study or comparative outcome data accompanies this claim.
qs: Those human interpreters are being paid $14 per hour to interpret many different languages.
It is true that sometimes humans also, if you don’t have the financial means to let them work properly, they will not serve citizens.
Those people are being served better today, even if it is not perfect, than by understaffed teams of underpaid human interpreters.

kp.k: Integrated interfaces should combine speed with selective expert scrutiny
kp.d: Reichenberg says Neur.on is working toward becoming an embedded translation component for other legal-tech tools because lawyers struggle with switching interfaces. Her envisioned workflow permits fast, good-enough processing followed by deeper examination of ambiguous items, illustrated by one unusual message among one million messages. Looking ahead a few years, she predicts consolidation around tools integrating best-in-class features in one interface.
qs: I think for translation, the obvious next step for us that we’re working on is becoming the brick for every single legal tech tool out there
lawyers are already struggling with the fact that they have to pilot so many different tools and jump from one to the other.
You want to be able to click and deep dive into the different meanings and be able to do that seamlessly.

I think there is going to be consolidation, of course, because the company that allows you to do what we were mentioning before, to get the best-in-class feature for everything in one place, that tool will be so popular.

kp.k: Mass-market provision may coexist with fewer premium specialists
kp.d: In her forward-looking response, Reichenberg uses Zola's depiction of department stores displacing small shops, alongside IKEA and luxury-fashion analogies, to anticipate legal-industry change. She expects fewer traditional craftspeople rather than their complete disappearance and sees benefits in mass-market provision alongside continued success for premium specialists. Her translation company's repositioning supplies the experiential analogy, not proof of the legal industry's future.
qs: I really see the legal industry going through the same phases as, I don’t know if in the US you read Émile Zola, probably not.
some old craftspeople become less numerous, because you still have wonderful hat makers, just fewer of them.
Now it is the luxury end of the industry, and it has a lot of success because of that.
So yes, I am looking forward to discovering the Loro Piana of both the law firms and the legal tech world.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Client self-service displaces routine work while highly specialized services can command premiums.
pts.d: Paula Reichenberg reports that machine translation eliminated easy assignments at Hieronymus, including work attracting urgency fees, and shifted the business toward premium specialization. She presents this experience as a possible trajectory for law firms, with fewer traditional bespoke providers and continuing demand at the luxury end.

pts.k: AI-generated contracts already replace some lawyer involvement despite lower quality.
pts.d: Reichenberg says lay counterparties recently supplied AI-generated contracts that previously would have involved lawyers. Her claim is not that AI matches professional quality, but that clients often accept mediocre outputs. She describes correcting provisions against her interests while retaining favorable ones.

pts.k: Legal AI's value depends on data, processes, and efficient human verification rather than error-free generation.
pts.d: Reichenberg argues that professionals see errors that lay users miss. She describes Neur.on as helping users identify and correct mistakes, rather than guaranteeing perfect output, and offers an illustrative reduction from sixteen hours of correction to four. This is an augmentation workflow with human checking before reliance.

pts.k: Basic chat dominates usage, limiting uptake of specialized productivity features.
pts.d: Reichenberg reports that users overwhelmingly use basic chat rather than specialized features that could save time. She says this forced greater investment in basic functionality, while intensive users more readily perceive the platform's added value.

pts.k: Some clients trust polished AI explanations more than professional advice.
pts.d: Reichenberg recounts a Swiss tax negotiation in which counterparties resisted a tax lawyer's explanation but accepted a ChatGPT answer after she corrected it. She uses this to describe a trust pattern, not to establish that the AI answer was superior.

pts.k: Legal technology will consolidate around integrated interfaces.
pts.d: Reichenberg predicts popularity and consolidation around tools integrating best-in-class functions in one interface. She says Neur.on is working toward supplying translation as an embedded component, allowing quick routine translation and deeper examination of ambiguous passages without changing tools.

pts.k: AI may produce tiered justice services while improving language access where human provision is inadequate.
pts.d: Reichenberg speculates that routine matters such as parking tickets could become a retail tier while human judging becomes a luxury offering. Separately, she claims that machine translation and language models already serve refugees better than understaffed, underpaid interpreting teams. Her access-to-justice optimism is qualified by imperfect technology and the poor resources available to the human comparator.

pts.k: Excellent multidisciplinary experts remain valuable and, in her account, are not replaceable by AI.
pts.d: Speaking specifically about her combination of lawyers, linguists, and engineers, Reichenberg asserts that these experts cannot be replaced by AI. She emphasizes expertise, excellence, teamwork, and trust between disciplines rather than making a universal employment forecast for lawyers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The market-displacement argument rests on her translation business experience and recent contract negotiations.
pts.d: Reichenberg cites changes in Hieronymus's work mix, its sale to a specialist-focused group, and personal dealings with lay contract drafters. These are firsthand business observations and an analogy to legal services, not quantified legal-market findings or a measured forecast.

pts.k: Productivity and adoption claims derive from product development and customer experience, without a specified study.
pts.d: The sixteen-to-four-hour comparison is a hypothetical customer counterfactual, not a reported controlled test. The eighty-percent usage figure has no disclosed sample, measurement period, or method. Her model-quality argument draws on building multilingual legal models and customer conversations. No benchmark results or independently measured model error rates are supplied.

pts.k: Trust and access claims are anecdotal; consolidation and tiered justice are predictions and analogies.
pts.d: Reichenberg supplies a personal Swiss tax negotiation example for AI trust. Her refugee-interpreting comparison includes an asserted hourly wage but no named study or comparative outcomes data. She extrapolates tiered judicial services from luxury versus retail translation and market restructuring from department-store and fashion analogies. The hosts' references to studies are not treated as her evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: She distinguishes observed translation changes and current legal self-service from longer-term legal-market predictions.
pts.d: Translation displacement is retrospective and connected to improving machine translation; AI contract self-service and reported usage patterns are current interview observations. Consolidation and the bespoke-provider analogy occur in response to a question about a few years ahead. No precise dates, market shares, or timetable for tiered judging are given. Integration is an active product direction, not a claim of universal deployment.

pts.k: Benefits and acceptable quality depend on the task, verification requirements, user experience, and available human resources.
pts.d: Reichenberg allows fast, good-enough output for some purposes but emphasizes correction before court submission. Users who have experienced difficult correction work are more likely to understand specialist tools' value. Her language-access comparison is against under-resourced human provision, not adequately funded expert interpretation. European legal AI also faces jurisdiction-specific languages and legal traditions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Routine providers lose work; specialist providers retain premium demand; clients assume more drafting and quality risk.
pts.d: Reichenberg describes translation agencies losing easy assignments and extrapolates pressure on traditional law firms. Highly specialized providers may thrive. Lay clients increasingly draft for themselves, potentially accepting adverse provisions they do not recognize. Lawyers handling machine output take on verification and correction work, with specialist tooling intended to reduce that burden.

pts.k: Lawyer users and technology suppliers face interface fragmentation and uneven feature adoption.
pts.d: Lawyers must switch among tools; integrated interfaces could reduce that friction. Legal-tech vendors face pressure to improve basic chat and integrate specialist functions, while Neur.on positions itself as an embedded translation supplier. Reichenberg sees continued value in multidisciplinary expert teams.

pts.k: Retail and premium clients may receive different service levels, while refugees may gain better interpreting access.
pts.d: Reichenberg contrasts private banks serving ultra-high-net-worth clients with retail providers willing to use machine translation. She extends that segmentation speculatively to judicial services. Refugees in Italian reception camps are her concrete example of people who may benefit from imperfect AI language services when existing human interpreting is inadequately resourced.
